principle_name: The Gap: Current State vs Future State Defines the Sale
author: Keenan
when_to_use: In every sale, as the foundational diagnostic framework — before pitching anything, the rep must understand where the customer is today (current state) and where they want to be (future state); the size of that gap determines the value of the deal.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to purely transactional, commodity purchases where the customer has already specified exactly what they need and there is no discovery to conduct.
principle: The formula that drives every sale is: Future State minus Current State equals the Gap. The bigger the gap, the bigger the deal. Salespeople do not sell products — they sell the change from a painful current state to a desired future state. If the customer cannot see the gap clearly, they will not buy, because people only buy when they believe the value of changing outweighs the cost of changing.
questions_to_ask: What does your current process / situation look like today?
What problems or limitations are you dealing with right now?
What would it look like if those problems were resolved?
What would solving this mean for your business in the next 12 months?
What is the specific goal or number you are trying to reach?
recommended_action: Before any pitch, fully map the customer's current state (facts, problems, root causes, impact, emotional state) and their desired future state (specific outcomes, measurable targets, intrinsic motivation). Only then calculate whether the gap is large enough to justify the investment of change.
example: An OEM's vendor development team is currently spending 3 weeks per new part qualification with significant rework costs. Their desired future state is a 1-week qualification cycle and zero rework. The gap represents significant cost savings — that is what the rep is selling, not the machining capability itself.
counter_example: Opening a meeting by presenting precision machining capabilities and tolerances without first understanding what specific problems the OEM is experiencing and what outcome they are trying to achieve.
motm_application: This is the master diagnostic framework for the MOTM AI Sales Director — every strategy recommendation should be structured around diagnosing the customer's current state, future state, and the gap between them before any pitch is generated. Feeds MOTM-K07 (Discovery), MOTM-K08 (First Meeting), and the 'Situation Analyzer' component of the architecture.

principle_name: Current State Has Five Elements — All Must Be Uncovered
author: Keenan
when_to_use: During every discovery conversation — as a checklist to ensure the rep has gone deep enough before moving to solution or proposal.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable when the customer has already provided all five elements unprompted — in that case, proceed to gap calculation rather than re-running the discovery.
principle: A complete picture of the customer's current state requires five distinct elements: (1) the literal physical facts about the business and environment; (2) the specific problems — not the customer's perceived needs, but the actual problems creating their pain; (3) the impact of those problems on the business; (4) the root causes of the problems; and (5) the customer's emotional state as they describe the situation. Missing any one of these elements leaves the rep with an incomplete diagnosis and a weak case for change.
questions_to_ask: Walk me through how this process works today.
What specifically is going wrong — and how often?
What is the impact of that on your output / revenue / timeline / people?
Why do you think this problem exists?
How are you and your team feeling about this situation?
recommended_action: Use the five-element checklist as a mental framework for every discovery: facts, problems, impact, root cause, emotional state. Do not move to solution or proposal until all five are clearly understood and documented.
example: For an OEM prospect: facts (CNC machining facility, 50 active part numbers), problems (delivery delays on 30% of orders), impact (production line stoppages costing 2 days/month), root cause (single-source supplier with no buffer capacity), emotional state (engineering head frustrated and worried about escalation to plant manager).
counter_example: Identifying the problem (delivery delays) and immediately pitching a solution without understanding the root cause, the business impact, or the emotional urgency driving the conversation.
motm_application: Directly drives the 'Situation Analyzer' component of the MOTM architecture (Section 21 of the brief) — the AI's situation classifier should be designed to extract all five current-state elements before generating any strategy output. Feeds MOTM-K07 (Discovery Process).

principle_name: You Are Selling Change, Not a Product
author: Keenan
when_to_use: As a foundational mindset for every sales interaction — the rep is never selling a product or service; they are selling the impact their solution will have on the customer's current environment.
when_not_to_use: Not a situational tactic — this is a permanent mental framework that governs how the rep thinks about every conversation, pitch, and objection.
principle: People do not buy products — they buy solutions to their problems and the outcomes those solutions enable. The product or service is merely the vehicle for change. The real thing being sold is the movement from a painful current state to a desired future state. A rep who leads with product features is selling the wrong thing; a rep who leads with the impact of those features on the customer's specific situation is selling what the customer actually wants to buy.
questions_to_ask: If this problem were solved, what would that mean for your business?
What would you be able to do that you can't do right now?
What's the cost of this problem to you today?
recommended_action: Before every pitch, presentation, or email, replace product-first language with outcome-first language: not 'our precision machined parts have tolerances of +/-0.001mm' but 'our process eliminates the rework cycle that is currently costing your team two days per batch.'
example: Instead of pitching a hydraulic manifold block's material specs, pitch the elimination of a specific assembly failure rate the OEM is currently experiencing — and quantify what that failure rate costs them per month.
counter_example: Opening a first meeting with a slide deck showing the company's capabilities, certifications, and equipment list — all of which describe the product, not the change it enables.
motm_application: Core framing principle for MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework), MOTM-K09 (Proposal Strategy), and the AI's 'Recommended Pitch' output — all generated pitches should lead with the change enabled, not the product delivered.

principle_name: Future State Must Be Quantified, Not Described
author: Keenan
when_to_use: During discovery, whenever the customer describes their desired future state in vague or qualitative terms — the rep must push for specific, measurable targets before proceeding.
when_not_to_use: When the customer genuinely cannot quantify the outcome yet (e.g. very early in the process) — accept what they can give and commit to revisiting.
principle: Vague future states produce vague gaps and unconvincing business cases. When a customer says they want 'better efficiency' or 'more growth,' that is not a future state — it is a wish. The future state must be expressed in specific, measurable terms (e.g. 'reduce part qualification time from 3 weeks to 1 week,' 'increase on-time delivery from 72% to 90%') so that the gap can be calculated precisely and the value of solving the problem is undeniable.
questions_to_ask: What would 'better' actually look like in numbers?
What specific percentage or figure are you trying to reach?
How much time / money / people would you save if this problem were solved?
What is your target for next year — and what needs to change to hit it?
recommended_action: Never accept a vague answer about the future state. After every qualitative answer, ask a quantifying follow-up: 'What does that mean specifically — give me a number.' Only stop when the future state is expressed in measurable terms that allow the gap to be calculated.
example: When a plant head says 'we need faster delivery,' ask 'what does fast mean to you — what lead time would you need to see?' until you get '3 weeks instead of 8 weeks.' That specific number is the future state.
counter_example: Accepting 'we want to be more competitive on lead times' as the future state and building a proposal without knowing what lead time the customer actually needs to achieve.
motm_application: Directly supports MOTM-K07 (Discovery Process) and the AI's classifier field 'missing_information' — the AI should flag any situation where the future state has not been quantified and recommend a follow-up question to close the gap before a strategy is generated.

principle_name: Credibility, Not Likability, Drives the Sale
author: Keenan
when_to_use: As a guiding mindset for every prospect interaction — especially relevant when a rep is spending disproportionate time on relationship-building activities (lunches, events, check-in calls) without advancing the sale.
when_not_to_use: Not a reason to be cold or transactional — basic professional rapport is still required; this principle addresses priority, not the complete elimination of interpersonal warmth.
principle: The widely held belief that 'people buy from people they like' is largely misleading: buyers buy from people they believe can solve their problems. Likeability gets you in the door; credibility gets you the deal. Credibility comes from demonstrating deep knowledge of the customer's industry, environment, and problems — and from asking questions that reveal an understanding of their world that most reps don't have. The best salespeople are the ones whose customers would consider hiring them as consultants.
questions_to_ask: What do I know about this customer's industry that they might not have considered?
Can I identify a problem in their business that they haven't yet recognized?
Am I bringing a specific insight to this conversation or just asking how things are going?
recommended_action: Prioritize industry and problem knowledge over social rapport-building. Invest preparation time in understanding the customer's business, their likely problems, and their industry context — and demonstrate that knowledge in every interaction rather than leading with personality.
example: A rep who opens a conversation by referencing a specific supply chain challenge typical in hydraulic OEM manufacturing — and asking a probing question about how the customer handles it — builds more credibility in five minutes than a rep who spent three months sending friendly check-in emails.
counter_example: Spending time and budget on entertainment and relationship activities with a prospect who has not yet converted, hoping that likeability will eventually tip the decision — without ever clearly diagnosing their problem.
motm_application: Core to MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework) and the hypothesis-based opening in the MOTM AI's 'Recommended Pitch' output — the AI should always lead with problem-specific insight, not generic capability claims or rapport-building openers.

principle_name: Get the Customer to Let You Help Them Before Selling Anything
author: Keenan
chapter: Chapter Seven: Get Them to Let You Help
when_to_use: At the very start of any new sales relationship — the rep's primary objective is not to pitch but to earn the customer's permission and trust to help them.
when_not_to_use: When the customer is already an inbound lead who has explicitly requested help — in that case they have already granted permission; proceed to discovery.
principle: No selling can happen until the customer is willing to open up, share information about their situation, and actively partner with the rep in finding a solution. Getting the customer to 'let you help them' is a pre-condition for discovery, and discovery is a pre-condition for a sale. The test is simple: are you hearing a series of 'yes' responses as the customer shares progressively more about their world? If not, stop advancing the sale and go back to building credibility.
questions_to_ask: Are they being open and forthcoming with information?
Are they asking questions that indicate engagement?
Are they agreeing to next steps that require effort on their side?
recommended_action: Measure every conversation not by whether the rep pitched the product, but by whether the customer demonstrated willingness to open up and share. If the customer is not providing information, not asking questions, and not agreeing to next steps, the rep has not yet earned the right to sell — refocus on demonstrating expertise and understanding their world.
example: A purchase manager who starts volunteering information about their quality rejection rates and asking 'what do you typically see in similar plants?' has granted permission to help. A purchase manager who says 'send me your brochure' has not.
counter_example: Pitching the product after a 10-minute introductory call because the rep ran out of questions — without having earned the customer's genuine engagement or willingness to share their real situation.
motm_application: Core for MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework) and MOTM-K06 (Sales Process) — the AI should flag situations where the customer is not demonstrating openness and recommend a credibility-building step before advancing the opportunity.

principle_name: Discovery Is Where the Sale Is Won or Lost — Not at the Close
author: Keenan
chapter: Chapter Eight: Discovery — Know Your Clients Better Than They Know Themselves
when_to_use: As a foundational mindset governing time allocation across the sales process — the rep should invest disproportionately in discovery relative to pitching and closing.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to purely transactional sales where the product is already specified and the decision is price-only.
principle: Research on over one million sales calls shows that the single biggest differentiator between won and lost deals is not the close — it is the quality of the discovery. In calls that led to closed deals, salespeople listened for over 50% of the time. In calls that led to lost deals, salespeople talked 80% of the time. Every additional question asked in the early sales cycle increases the probability of closing the deal. The sale is won at the beginning, not the end.
questions_to_ask: Am I learning more from this conversation than the customer is?
Have I spoken less than the customer in this meeting?
Do I know more about their situation now than when we started?
recommended_action: Redesign meeting preparation around discovery objectives rather than pitch objectives: prepare 10-15 questions before any meeting, commit to listening for more than 50% of the conversation, and measure meeting success by how much current-state information was gathered rather than how many product features were presented.
example: A rep who spends 45 minutes asking probing, process, and provoking questions in a first meeting and takes 5 minutes to briefly introduce their company at the end will consistently outperform a rep who delivers a 40-minute capability presentation.
counter_example: Starting a first meeting with a 20-minute company and product presentation, then asking 'so what challenges are you facing?' — by which point the customer has mentally checked out.
motm_application: Core to MOTM-K07 (Discovery Process) and MOTM-K08 (First Meeting Framework) — the AI's first-meeting recommendations should always prioritize discovery questions over product presentation, and the standard response template should include a 'Questions to Ask' section that is longer than the 'Pitch' section in early-stage situations.

principle_name: Problem-Centric Discovery: Four Question Types for Going Deep
author: Keenan
when_to_use: Throughout every discovery conversation — as a structured question framework for uncovering the five elements of the current state.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable as a rigid script — this is a framework for thinking about question types, not a checklist to run through in order.
principle: Effective discovery uses four types of questions in combination: (1) Probing questions — open-ended questions that press for specific facts and details ('tell me about...', 'help me understand...', 'walk me through...'); (2) Process questions — questions that ask how things are actually done, step by step, to reveal operational inefficiencies; (3) Provoking questions — questions that challenge customers to think about their situation from a new angle, often uncovering problems they had not recognized; (4) Validating questions — confirmations that the rep has correctly understood what the customer said, preventing misdiagnosis.
questions_to_ask: Tell me about how you currently manage [X].
Walk me through the steps your team takes when [Y] happens.
What if you could no longer do [Z] — what would the impact be?
What I'm hearing is [summary] — did I get that right?
Has there ever been a time when [scenario]? What happened?
recommended_action: Prepare a mix of all four question types before every discovery call. Lead with probing questions to gather facts, follow with process questions to understand how things work, use provoking questions to expand the customer's awareness of their own problems, and confirm understanding throughout with validating questions.
example: Probing: 'Tell me about your current approval process for new suppliers.' Process: 'Walk me through each step from first contact to approved vendor status.' Provoking: 'What happens to your production schedule when a new supplier approval takes longer than expected?' Validating: 'So what I'm hearing is that the approval bottleneck costs you 4-6 weeks on average — is that right?'
counter_example: Asking only surface-level probing questions and accepting the first answer given — moving to the pitch as soon as the customer mentions a problem, without understanding its impact, root cause, or true magnitude.
motm_application: Directly informs the 'Questions to Ask' section of MOTM's standard response template — the AI should generate all four question types for every discovery situation, clearly labeled by purpose.

principle_name: Never Accept an Open-Ended Answer — Quantify Everything
author: Keenan
when_to_use: Every time a customer gives a vague, qualitative, or unquantified answer to a discovery question — the rep must press for a specific number before moving on.
when_not_to_use: When the customer genuinely cannot quantify (e.g. 'I don't have that data to hand') — accept the limitation, note it, and follow up rather than blocking the conversation.
principle: Open-ended, unquantified answers are insufficient for gap selling because they cannot be used to calculate the gap or build a compelling business case. 'We're not growing fast enough' tells you nothing useful; '22% growth when we need 25%' gives you a 3% gap you can price a solution against. Every problem, impact, and future state must be expressed in specific, measurable terms — otherwise the rep is guessing at the value of what they are selling.
questions_to_ask: What does 'fast enough' mean in numbers?
Can you give me a specific figure?
How much time / money / output is this costing you?
What is the target number you're trying to reach?
recommended_action: After every vague answer, ask a quantifying follow-up immediately: 'Define that for me — what does [vague word] mean in specific terms?' Do not proceed to the next question until a number, percentage, or measurable outcome is provided.
example: Customer says: 'Our delivery performance isn't great.' Rep responds: 'Define that for me — what percentage on-time delivery are you achieving today, and what would you need it to be?' Customer: '68%, and we need 90% to meet our OEM contract requirements.' Now the rep has a quantified gap of 22 percentage points.
counter_example: Accepting 'delivery performance isn't great' and building a proposal around 'improving delivery' — without knowing whether the customer needs 80%, 90%, or 99% on-time performance, or what the financial penalty for missing the current rate is.
motm_application: Core to MOTM-K07 (Discovery Process) and the AI's response template — the 'My Read of the Situation' section should always flag unquantified gaps as missing information requiring follow-up before a full strategy can be generated.

principle_name: Technical Problems Start Conversations; Business Problems Drive Sales
author: Keenan
when_to_use: During discovery, whenever the conversation is stuck at a technical level — the rep must push beyond the technical symptom to the business consequence before a deal can be advanced.
when_not_to_use: Not a reason to skip technical understanding entirely — the technical problem must be understood as the root cause; this principle governs the level at which the case for change is made, not whether technical details matter.
principle: There are two layers to every problem: the technical problem (a process, system, or capability that isn't working correctly) and the business problem (the financial, operational, or strategic consequence of the technical problem). Every prospect can have the same technical problem, but no two prospects have the same business problem. Technical problems are conversation starters; business problems are the source of buying motivation. The rep who only diagnoses the technical problem will lose to the rep who reaches the business problem — because the business problem is where the emotional urgency and buying decision live.
questions_to_ask: What is the business impact of that technical limitation?
What does that problem cost you in output / revenue / time / headcount?
If that technical limitation were eliminated, what would change about the business?
recommended_action: In every discovery, use the technical problem as a starting point and then immediately push to the business consequence: 'So the system doesn't integrate — what does that mean for your team in terms of time and cost?' Do not stop at the technical level when building the business case.
example: Technical problem: 'Our CNC supplier's tolerances are inconsistent.' Business problem: 'We're spending 15% of production time on incoming inspection and rework, costing approximately ₹40L per year and delaying our assembly line by an average of 2 days per batch.' The business problem drives the sale; the technical problem merely confirms it exists.
counter_example: Proposing a supplier switch based solely on the technical problem (tolerance inconsistency) without discovering what that inconsistency costs the customer — leaving the business case unbuilt and the decision unmotivated.
motm_application: Core for MOTM-K15 (OEM Selling) and MOTM-K09 (Proposal Strategy) — the AI should always push discovery recommendations from the technical problem level to the business problem level, and proposals should be framed around business consequences rather than technical specifications.

principle_name: The Problem Identification Chart: Know the Problems Before the Call
author: Keenan
when_to_use: Before approaching any prospect — as a pre-call preparation tool that maps the likely problems, their business impacts, and their root causes for a given customer type or industry vertical.
when_not_to_use: Not a substitute for actual discovery — the PIC prepares hypotheses, not conclusions. The actual problems must be confirmed through conversation with the customer.
principle: The best salespeople identify their customers' likely problems before picking up the phone or writing an email, rather than waiting to discover them in the meeting. A Problem Identification Chart maps three columns for each solvable problem: the problem itself, the likely business impact on the customer, and what the rep knows about the root cause. This preparation allows the rep to open conversations with specific, relevant hypotheses rather than generic questions — building immediate credibility and giving the prospect a reason to engage.
recommended_action: Before approaching any target account type (e.g. OEM purchase manager, precision machining buyer, distributor head), complete a Problem Identification Chart listing 5-10 likely problems your product/service solves, the typical business impact of each, and the most common root causes. Use this to shape your outreach message and your discovery opening hypothesis.
example: For a MOTM Sales Engineer approaching a hydraulic OEM: Problem — extended new supplier qualification time. Impact — delayed production launches, competitive pressure, engineering resource drain. Root cause — manual documentation process with no digital supplier portal. The outreach message leads with the problem, not the product.
counter_example: Cold calling an OEM purchase manager with 'We are a precision machining supplier with ISO 9001 certification and competitive pricing' — a message that offers no hypothesis about their problems and gives them no reason to engage.
motm_application: Directly maps to MOTM-K15 (OEM Selling), MOTM-K16 (Distributor Development), and the Customer Website Analyzer in the MOTM architecture — the AI should generate a Problem Identification Chart as part of account entry strategy outputs, using the customer's website data and industry context to hypothesize likely problems.

principle_name: The Gap Calculation: Future State Minus Current State Determines Deal Value
author: Keenan
chapter: Chapter Nine: Is the Gap Worth It?
when_to_use: After completing discovery — as the final qualification step before investing in a proposal or solution presentation.
when_not_to_use: Before discovery is complete — the gap cannot be calculated without both a quantified current state and a quantified future state.
principle: Once both the current state and future state are quantified, the gap can be calculated as a specific number — and that number tells the rep whether the deal is worth pursuing at the proposed investment level. A customer wanting to go from 10% to 20% growth represents a $10M gap if their revenue is $100M. The question the rep must then ask is: is this gap large enough that the customer would pay for your solution? If the gap is large relative to the investment, the deal is live. If the gap is too small, widen it through additional discovery or exit the deal — do not push through a sale that isn't justified by the gap.
questions_to_ask: Given the gap we've identified, does the investment make sense relative to the value of closing it?
Are there additional areas of impact we haven't yet discovered that would widen the gap?
Is the customer's sense of urgency proportional to the size of the gap?
recommended_action: After quantifying current state and future state, explicitly calculate the gap and present it to the customer before presenting a solution: 'Based on what you've told me, the gap between where you are and where you need to be is approximately X — is that how you see it?' Confirm agreement on the gap before presenting the investment required to close it.
example: Customer is at 72% on-time delivery and needs 90% to maintain their OEM contract. The gap is 18 percentage points. Penalty for losing the OEM contract: ₹2 Cr/year. The supplier's solution costs ₹15L/year. The gap justifies the investment by a ratio of 13:1.
counter_example: Presenting a proposal without first confirming that both parties agree on the size of the gap — leaving the customer to do their own (often incorrect) assessment of whether the investment is justified.
motm_application: Core to MOTM-K09 (Proposal Strategy) and MOTM-K10 (Pricing Rules) — the AI should always include a gap calculation in its strategy output for proposal-stage situations, and should not recommend a proposal if the gap has not been quantified.

principle_name: Intrinsic Motivation: Understand Why the Customer Wants to Change
author: Keenan
chapter: Chapter Ten: Know Your Customers' Why
when_to_use: After establishing the current state, future state, and gap — as the final discovery layer that reveals the personal, strategic, or organizational motivation driving the decision.
when_not_to_use: Before the customer has shared their current and future states — intrinsic motivation questions too early feel presumptuous and out of context.
principle: Behind every future state goal is a deeper motivation — a strategic commitment, a personal stake, a competitive pressure, or a timeline that makes the outcome non-negotiable. A customer who wants 20% growth may have that number because it is their commitment to a private equity investor, or because hitting it triggers a personal bonus, or because missing it means layoffs. The rep who knows the intrinsic motivation can customize the sale around what the customer is truly protecting or pursuing — which is always more powerful than the stated goal alone.
questions_to_ask: Tell me a bit about what is driving this change.
What happens if you don't hit this goal?
Why is this the right time to solve this?
What does achieving this mean for you personally — or for your team?
recommended_action: After summarizing the current state and future state back to the customer, ask: 'Tell me a bit about what is driving this change.' Listen carefully — the answer will reveal the real motivation and allow the rep to frame the solution in terms of what the customer is personally committed to protecting or achieving.
example: A plant head says they need to improve supplier reliability. The intrinsic motivation: the plant's performance is being reviewed by the corporate group next quarter and a major supply failure last year is still under scrutiny. The rep who knows this frames their solution around audit-readiness and management reporting, not just delivery metrics.
counter_example: Treating the stated goal (90% on-time delivery) as the complete picture and pitching only to that metric — missing the personal and organizational stakes that would make the customer feel the urgency to act now.
motm_application: Directly feeds the 'What Is Probably Happening' and 'Recommended Strategy' sections of MOTM's standard response template — the AI should always probe for intrinsic motivation and incorporate it into strategy recommendations, particularly for stuck or low-urgency opportunities.

principle_name: Four Qualification Questions: The Only Test That Matters
author: Keenan
when_to_use: At the end of every discovery conversation — as a four-question test to determine whether the opportunity is genuinely qualified before investing in a proposal or demo.
when_not_to_use: Not a replacement for B.A.N.T. mechanics entirely in organizations that require formal qualification fields — but the answers to these four questions are far more predictive of deal outcome than budget, authority, need, and timing checked in isolation.
principle: An opportunity is qualified when the rep can answer yes to all four of these questions: (1) Does the prospect have a problem you can fix? (2) Does the prospect agree they have a problem? (3) Does the prospect want to fix the problem? (4) Will the prospect go on a journey with you to fix the problem? If any answer is no, the opportunity is not qualified — and advancing it wastes time for both parties. This framework is more reliable than B.A.N.T. because it focuses on the customer's problem-awareness and willingness to change rather than on administrative factors like budget approval status.
questions_to_ask: Has the customer confirmed they recognize the problem?
Has the customer expressed genuine desire to resolve it?
Is the customer actively sharing information and engaging in discovery?
Is the customer agreeing to next steps that require their own effort?
recommended_action: After every discovery conversation, run the four-question test before advancing the deal stage. If any question is 'no,' identify which one and focus the next interaction on resolving that specific gap — do not skip ahead to proposal or demo.
example: A prospect who shares their delivery problem, confirms it is causing real production costs, expresses urgency to fix it before their next OEM review, and agrees to involve their engineering team in a technical assessment has passed all four questions — the opportunity is qualified.
counter_example: Advancing an opportunity to the proposal stage because the customer is 'interested' and has a budget — without confirming they agree they have a problem, want to fix it, and are willing to actively participate in the solution process.
motm_application: Directly feeds MOTM-K05 (Lead Qualification) — the AI should use these four questions as the qualification framework in its strategy output rather than B.A.N.T., and should flag which of the four questions has not been answered when assessing a situation.

principle_name: The Sale Is a Staircase, Not a Straight Line — Focus on the Next Yes
author: Keenan
chapter: Chapter Twelve: Move Your Deals Through the Pipeline
when_to_use: Throughout the entire sales process — as the operating principle for pipeline management and deal advancement.
when_not_to_use: Not a tactic for a specific stage — this is a pipeline philosophy that governs how the rep thinks about progress at every stage of the sale.
principle: A sale is not a linear progression from first contact to close — it is a staircase of small yeses, each one representing the customer's renewed agreement to keep moving forward with the rep. Every time the customer agrees to something (share information, involve another stakeholder, attend a meeting, review a proposal) that is a small sale within the sale. The rep's job at every stage is not to close the big deal — it is to identify and win the next small yes. If the customer is not saying yes to anything, the deal is not progressing regardless of how much effort the rep is investing.
questions_to_ask: What is the next thing I need the customer to agree to?
What would make the customer willing to take that next step?
Is the customer investing equal effort in this process, or am I the only one doing the work?
recommended_action: At the end of every customer interaction, identify the specific next yes needed and make winning it the objective of the next touchpoint. A healthy deal shows the customer's effort rising in parallel with the rep's — if the rep is doing all the work and the customer is passive, the deal is at risk.
example: In an OEM account entry situation, the next yes might be 'will they agree to a technical meeting with engineering?' — not 'will they place a trial order?' The rep's energy should go into earning the technical meeting, not skipping ahead to the order.
counter_example: Following up repeatedly with 'just checking in' emails after a proposal is submitted — investing effort into activity that does not represent a specific next yes and does not advance the deal.
motm_application: Core to MOTM-K12 (Follow-Up Framework) and MOTM-K13 (Closing) — the AI's 'Immediate Next Action' in the standard response template should always be a specific, named next yes rather than a generic follow-up instruction.
